# Block 8: AI-assisted code review {.unnumbered} You will hand a script to an AI reviewer and grade what it finds. Because you already know this script's twelve problems, you can measure the machine rather than trust it. :::{.callout-note} **Before you start.** You need the OSF project folder from (`ANALYSIS.R` and its data) and your P1–P12 catalogue from the [manual code-review chapter](07-code-review.qmd), which is the answer key. No catalogue? Your instructor shares it after Part 3; don't look before your review has run. ::: *⏱ ~40 minutes* ## Part 1: What AI is, and is not, good for in code review {#ai-why} *⏱ ~5 minutes* An AI reviewer reads every line and never tires, but it sounds equally sure whether it is right or wrong. Here is where to expect help, on the four Rs of code review (Ivimey-Cook et al., 2023): ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
AI capability mapped onto the four Rs
R AI is likely to be... Why
Reported Useful for drafting It can summarise what the script appears to do and flag missing documentation or undocumented exclusions. It cannot know the intended analysis unless you state it.
Run Strong, if it can execute An agent that runs the script in a fresh R session can show whether it runs. A chat window can only predict, and its prediction can read as though it ran the code.
Reliable Weak Silent semantic errors (P4 precedence, P8 sentinel, P9 incomparable models, P10 wrong family) depend on context. Expect some caught, some missed and some invented, all in the same confident tone.
Reproducible Mixed It can flag a missing lockfile or session record. It can confirm that results reproduce only by running the code and comparing outputs.
````` ::: ::: **The rule:** treat every AI finding as a claim to check, and the absence of a finding as no evidence that the problem is absent. Used that way, AI review is reliably good for: - summarising what an unfamiliar script does; - flagging missing documentation, unexplained filters and hard-coded paths; - finding run errors, when it can actually execute the code; - a second pair of eyes that never tires on line 300. So next week, run your saved review prompt on a script before you share it, and spend your own attention on the *Reliable* questions. In software engineering, developers acted on about three-quarters of an AI reviewer's comments but saw only minor gains in quality, and the reviewer did worse when it was not told what the code was meant to do (Cihan et al., 2025; Cihan, 2025). Nobody has measured it on analysis scripts like this one, which is what you will do. :::{.callout-note} **Opening poll** *(type in chat)* "If an AI code reviewer told you your analysis was clean, would you trust it enough to submit?" A: Yes, it read every line B: Only if I had also read it myself C: No, I would trust my own review over the AI's D: I would trust it for *Run*, not for *Reliable* Keep the result visible; we return to it at the end. ::: ## Part 2: Telling the AI how to behave {#ai-prompting} *⏱ ~10 minutes* "Review my code" gets a vague, generous review. A good review prompt has four parts: | Part | Why | |---|---| | **A role and a standard**: "a critical reviewer applying the four Rs" | Gives the output a structure you can check | | **The intended analysis**: the model from the OSF page, with `TO` a count and block `B` a random effect | Without it, the AI cannot see that a Gaussian `lmer()` is the wrong family (P10) | | **No flattery**: line number, which R, severity, a fix | Keeps it to findings you can act on | | **Honest uncertainty**: "NEEDS HUMAN CHECK" instead of guessing | Shows you where to look yourself | :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Write the review prompt (7 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **1. Start from the draft** below and check it has all four parts. **2. Split the room.** Surnames A–M are **Group A** and keep the line about the 9999 sentinel valueA number with a special meaning, such as 9999 for “not recorded” or -1 for “run failed”. It must be documented in a codebook and recoded before analysis.; N–Z are **Group B** and delete it. Everything else stays the same. **3. Keep it.** In your **workshop** project, run `usethis::edit_file("docs/review-prompt.md")` in the R console, paste your prompt and save. You will reuse it after the course. **You are done when** your prompt has all four elements and is saved in `docs/review-prompt.md`.
**Prompt (Claude Code, or a chat window):** ```text You are a critical code reviewer for an evolutionary-biology journal. Review ANALYSIS.R using the four Rs: Reported, Run, Reliable, Reproducible. The intended analysis (from the pre-registration) is: total offspring (TO, a count: non-negative integer, often overdispersed) modelled as TO ~ strain * diet + (1 | B), with block B as a random effect. Rules: - Do NOT praise the code. Report only problems. - For each issue: line number(s), which R it violates, severity (critical / high / medium), and a concrete one-line fix. - The raw data use 9999 as a "not recorded" code. Check whether this is handled. <- Group B: delete this line - Flag anything you CANNOT determine by reading alone as "NEEDS HUMAN CHECK" rather than guessing. - If you are uncertain about a finding, say so explicitly. Organise your output by the four Rs. ```
:::: ::: ## Part 3: Running the review {#ai-running} *⏱ ~25 minutes* ### Path A: Claude Code, read-only For the A/B comparison to work, the agentAn assistant that can read across a project’s files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises. must see the script and nothing else; with the data it would find the 9999 code by itself. **1. Copy the script into an empty project.** With the OSF project open, in the R console: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} usethis::create_project("~/ai-review", open = FALSE) fs::file_copy(here::here("ANALYSIS.R"), "~/ai-review/ANALYSIS.R") ``` ::: Then open `~/ai-review` in a new window: in RStudio, *File → Open Project in New Session*; in Positron, *File → New Window* and open the folder there. **2. Start Claude Code there.** In the new window's Terminal tab: ```bash claude ``` This folder has none of your workshop settings, so Claude Code starts in its own default, `auto`. Starting your request with `/plan` keeps it to reading (rungOne level of the autonomy ladder in Block 4, from suggesting a line (rung 0) to acting with no prompts (rung 5). Each step up removes a moment when you would have seen an action before it happened. 2 in [Block 4](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd)). **3. Ask for the review.** Type `/plan`, a space, then paste your prompt. **4. Save the review.** `plan` mode writes no files, so copy the review into a text file yourself. **You are done when** you have the review saved in a file. **If it goes wrong:** if Claude Code lists data files, you started it in the OSF project window, not the `ai-review` one: `/exit`, switch windows and start again. If you have no agent, use Path B. :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Using Posit Assistant Open the folder holding only `ANALYSIS.R` in RStudio or Positron, and switch Posit Assistant to Ask mode, so it can read but not change anything. Give it your Part 2 prompt and copy the review into a file yourself. For the optional step below, open the full OSF project folder and use Normal mode, so it asks before running anything. ::: ### Path A, step 2: let it run the script (optional) An agent that can run R turns the *Run* question from a prediction into evidence. The script needs its data, so `/exit`, switch to the OSF project's window and start `claude` in its Terminal tab. This folder starts in `auto` too: press `Shift+Tab` until it shows Manual (`default`), so it asks before running anything. **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text Run ANALYSIS.R from a fresh R session with Rscript and report the exact output and any errors. Do not install packages; if a package is missing, report which one. Do not edit any file. ``` Read the approval prompt, then the output. "The script runs" counts only if you can see the command and its output in the conversation; without them it is a claimed executionA statement that code runs or reproduces, made without the command that was run and the output it produced. Treat it as a prediction, not evidence.. A missing package is a finding about your machine, not about the code. ### Path B: chat window If you have no agent, paste the whole of `ANALYSIS.R` into any chat window, followed by your Part 2 prompt. Paste the script only, not the data. :::{.callout-warning} A chat window cannot run anything, but its answer to "does this run?" can read as though it did. Ask "what would *prevent* this running?" instead. ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Grade the machine (10 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **1. Score the review.** Open your P1–P12 catalogue beside the AI's review: - **Hits:** which of P1–P12 did it identify correctly? - **Misses:** which did it miss? Look especially at P4 (precedence) and P8 (sentinel), the silent, consequential ones. - **False positives:** what did it flag that is not a real problem, or describe wrongly? Each one is a false positiveIn a code review, a problem the AI reports confidently that is not real, or describes wrongly.. - **Execution claims:** did it claim the script runs or reproduces? On what evidence? **2. Post your result.** In the chat, post your group (A or B), your hit count, your most consequential miss and your most confident false positive, with line numbers. **3. Decide.** Which one finding would you act on first, and what would you check before acting on it? **You are done when** every P1–P12 problem is marked hit or miss, and you have listed the false positives. **If it goes wrong:** if your review never arrived, grade a neighbour's review posted in the chat; the comparison works the same way. :::: ::: :::{.callout-note} ## Debrief (5 minutes) 1. Compare P8 hit rates between Groups A and B. Only the data and your knowledge reveal that 9999 is a code: what does that say about reviewing code without the data? 2. Whose AI produced the most confident false positive? 3. Did any agent claim the script runs without having run it? 4. Back to the opening poll: would you change your answer? ::: :::{.callout-note} ## Check · Reproduce · Record - **You can now:** hand a script to an AI reviewer with a prompt that makes its output checkable, **trusted because** you grade it against problems you already know, and treat every finding as a claim. - **Check:** grade every AI finding against the P1–P12 answer key; the absence of a finding is no evidence that the problem is absent. - **Reproduce:** a claim that the script runs counts only with the command and the output from a fresh R session; to run one yourself, see [checking work](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd#checking-work). - **Record:** add a line to `docs/ai-log.md` in your workshop repository: the tool, its hit count and its most confident false positive. An AI-assisted README for the OSF project is in *Going further*. ::: ## Check your understanding **An AI reviewer reports that `ANALYSIS.R` "runs without errors". What do you need before treating that as evidence?**
**Why did Group A catch P8 more often than Group B?**
## Going further (not covered live) This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you. ### Copilot code review on a pull request If your repository is on GitHub, open a pull request containing `ANALYSIS.R` and request Copilot as a reviewer. Its comments appear on the changed lines, like a colleague's. It reads the repository's instruction files (`.github/copilot-instructions.md`, or `AGENTS.md` as in [Block 5](11e-instructions-skills.qmd)), but none of those exist in the OSF folder yet. To have Copilot apply the standard from Part 2, add your review rules (the four Rs, the intended analysis, no praise, NEEDS HUMAN CHECK) to `.github/copilot-instructions.md` in that repository before you request the review. ### Generating the README with AI {#ai-readme} *⏱ ~20 minutes* The second deliverable is the documentation that makes *Reported* and *Run* answerable: a README. You are provided with the `research-readme` skill: a `SKILL.md`, two helper scripts and a template. **Install the skill before you start.** Download the bundle and unzip it into the OSF project folder at `.agents/skills/`, so that the folder `.agents/skills/research-readme/` contains `SKILL.md`, `scripts/` and `references/`. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: - **Posit Assistant and GitHub Copilot** read `.agents/skills/` directly. - **Claude Code** reads `.claude/skills/`. Link or copy the folder there, as described in [Block 5](11e-instructions-skills.qmd). - **Chat window:** you do not need to install anything. You will run the two scripts yourself and paste the template into the chat. Check that the skill is visible before going on. In Claude Code, type `/` and look for `research-readme`. In any tool, the test is behaviour: when you invoke `/research-readme` in Pass 2, its first reply should be the numbered plan that the skill's "Before executing" section requires. If it is not, the skill did not load. **Put the folder under version control first.** A folder downloaded from OSF is not a git repository, so there would be nothing to compare the README against. With the OSF project open in RStudio or Positron, run `usethis::use_git()` in the R console and let it make the first commit. You run this in two passes. The first shows the failure; the second shows the fix. #### Pass 1: README from the AI alone (~4 minutes) Give the AI only `ANALYSIS.R` and the data, and ask for a README with no constraints. The result reads as complete. It will assign plausible units, describe variables it cannot have verified, and may state package versions it has no way to know. Note what it asserts about the variables and dependencies; Pass 2 replaces each guess with a fact you generate. #### Pass 2: README from verifiable inputs The skill's rules are that the AI must **not fabricate metadata**, and that automatic summaries **describe; they do not interpret**. So you generate the facts mechanically, and the AI only assembles and phrases them. ##### Step 1: Generate the inputs yourself (R, not AI) **In the R console**, with the OSF project open in RStudio or Positron (so that `here::here()` points at it, not at your workshop repository): ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} skill_dir <- here::here(".agents", "skills", "research-readme", "scripts") source(file.path(skill_dir, "describe_csv.R")) # type, missing count and range per column, printed in full for pasting describe_project_csvs(here::here()) |> print(n = Inf, width = Inf) source(file.path(skill_dir, "scan_packages.R")) print_lockfile(here::here("renv.lock")) # R and package versions, or a finding ``` ::: This project has no `renv.lock`. `scan_packages.R` reports that as an explicit finding rather than an error, and the README must say so. You cannot pin versions you never recorded. Look at the offspring column in the summary: its range will read something like `2 to 9999`. The 9999 code (P8) is a real number in the file, and the summary reports it without judgement. Judging plausibility is your job. That honest, uninterpreted range is the visible trace of the sentinel. ##### Step 2: Hand the AI the specification and the inputs **Agent path:** invoke `/research-readme` and let its five stages run. It will ask you for what it cannot find. **Chat path:** paste the structure from `references/readme_template.md` and the output you just generated, with this prompt: **Prompt (chat window):** ```text Draft a research README.md for this analysis repository, using exactly the sections in the template I paste below, in order. Use ONLY the facts I provide. Do not invent DOIs, ORCIDs, units or package versions. Where a value is missing, insert a visible placeholder: **TODO: supply [field]: not provided** Per-column summaries: [paste describe_project_csvs() output] Dependencies: [paste print_lockfile() output] Run order: ANALYSIS.R (the only analysis script in the folder). Add an AI declaration stating that an AI assisted in drafting this README, naming the model and today's date. Make no claims about AI use elsewhere. ``` :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Audit the README (10 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} Audit the draft against three of the skill's rules: 1. **No fabrication.** Pick three facts. Can you trace each to an input you gave? If not, it is invented. 2. **Describe, do not interpret.** Did the AI assign units or meanings you did not supply? Did the `2 to 9999` range survive, or was it "tidied" into something plausible and wrong? 3. **README only.** The Git pane should show that nothing except `README.md` changed since the commit you made before Pass 1. Note the worst fabrication or interpretation you caught, and whether the README's offspring range alone would have led you back to P8. The AI declarationA statement, for example in a README, recording that an AI assisted, naming the tool, model and date, and making no claim about AI use beyond what was recorded. should say no more than you told it. :::: ::: #### The skill bundle The bundle you downloaded above is reproduced here for reference; you do not need to edit it. Read it before you use it, as you would any skill you did not write. ``` research-readme/ ├── SKILL.md ├── scripts/ │ ├── describe_csv.R │ └── scan_packages.R └── references/ └── readme_template.md ``` :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ### `scripts/describe_csv.R` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # describe_csv.R ---- # Purpose: one row per column of a CSV file: name, the type readr assigns, # missing-value count, and a brief range (numeric) or distinct-value count # (other). Describes; does not interpret. # Used by: research-readme skill, Stage 2. describe_range <- function(x) { if (all(is.na(x))) { return("all values missing") } if (is.numeric(x)) { return(paste(min(x, na.rm = TRUE), "to", max(x, na.rm = TRUE))) } paste(dplyr::n_distinct(x, na.rm = TRUE), "distinct values") } # one-row-per-column summary of a single CSV ---- describe_csv <- function(path) { stopifnot(is.character(path), length(path) == 1L, file.exists(path)) data_df <- readr::read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE) tibble::tibble( file = basename(path), column = names(data_df), type = purrr::map_chr(data_df, \(x) class(x)[1]), n_missing = purrr::map_int(data_df, \(x) sum(is.na(x))), range = purrr::map_chr(data_df, describe_range), # completed by the user during Stage 2: description = NA_character_, unit = NA_character_ ) } # describe every CSV in a project, skipping renv and git folders ---- describe_project_csvs <- function(project_dir) { stopifnot(dir.exists(project_dir)) csv_paths <- list.files( project_dir, pattern = "\\.csv$", recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE, ignore.case = TRUE ) csv_paths <- csv_paths[!grepl("(^|/)(renv|\\.git)/", csv_paths)] if (length(csv_paths) == 0L) { message("No CSV files found under ", project_dir) return(tibble::tibble()) } csv_paths |> purrr::map(describe_csv) |> purrr::list_rbind() } ``` ::: ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ### `scripts/scan_packages.R` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scan_packages.R ---- # Purpose: read renv.lock and report the R version and pinned package # versions. A missing lockfile is reported as a finding, not an error. # Used by: research-readme skill, Stage 4. read_lockfile <- function(lock_path = "renv.lock") { if (!file.exists(lock_path)) { return(list(found = FALSE, r_version = NA_character_, packages = tibble::tibble())) } lock <- jsonlite::read_json(lock_path) packages <- purrr::pluck(lock, "Packages", .default = list()) packages_df <- tibble::tibble( package = unname(purrr::map_chr(packages, \(p) purrr::pluck(p, "Package", .default = NA_character_))), version = unname(purrr::map_chr(packages, \(p) purrr::pluck(p, "Version", .default = NA_character_))) ) |> dplyr::arrange(package) list( found = TRUE, r_version = purrr::pluck(lock, "R", "Version", .default = NA_character_), packages = packages_df ) } print_lockfile <- function(lock_path = "renv.lock") { info <- read_lockfile(lock_path) if (!info$found) { cat( "No lockfile found at ", lock_path, ".\n", "FINDING: package versions were not recorded.\n", "README text: **TODO: supply R version and key package versions: ", "not recorded; resolve before submission**\n", sep = "" ) return(invisible(info)) } cat("R version: ", info$r_version, "\n\n", sep = "") print(info$packages, n = Inf) invisible(info) } ``` ::: ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ### `SKILL.md` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` markdown --- name: research-readme description: >- Writes a README.md for a research repository whose code and data accompany a paper. Use when asked to write a README for an analysis project, document a repository for a paper, or prepare code for journal submission or archiving (Zenodo, Figshare, OSF). Not for general software READMEs and not for auditing code. disable-model-invocation: true --- # Research README generator Produces one README.md for a repository of R code and data that accompanies a manuscript, including the metadata that journals and archives expect: persistent identifiers, ORCIDs, funding, per-variable descriptions with units, an explicit script run order, and a dependency record. ## Operating constraints These hold for the whole conversation unless the user explicitly withdraws them. 1. The only file you create or overwrite is README.md. Do not edit, rename or delete any other file. If you notice an apparent error in code or data, record it under "Open questions" in the README or report it in chat, and leave the file untouched. 2. Do not fabricate metadata. DOIs, ORCIDs, grant numbers, collection dates, units and affiliations come from the user or from a file the user points to. If a value is unknown, insert a placeholder (see Placeholders). 3. Automatic summaries describe; they do not interpret. Report column type, missing count and range. Do not state what a variable means, its unit, or whether a value is plausible. 4. Work conversationally and write the file directly; do not build an app. ## Before executing Present a short numbered plan: the folder to be scanned, that only README.md will be written, and the five stages below. Wait for the user to confirm. ## Stage 1: Project information Collect title, abstract, DOIs (paper; archived code and data), licences, authors with ORCIDs and affiliations, and funders with grant numbers. Read these from CITATION.cff, codemeta.json or DESCRIPTION if present, and ask only for what is missing. Pair each author with their own ORCID and affiliation. If no code licence is supplied, flag it prominently and use a placeholder; do not choose a licence for the user. ## Stage 2: Files and variable summaries List the data and code files. For CSV files, run describe_project_csvs() from scripts/describe_csv.R and use its output as a scaffold. Ask the user for each column's description and unit, and for collection dates and locations per data file. List other tabular formats (.xlsx, .tsv) and ask the user to describe their columns by hand. Never infer units from column names. ## Stage 3: Script order List executable files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd). Propose a run order using numeric prefixes (01_, 02_) as the first signal, and ask the user to confirm or reorder; the user's order is authoritative. Collect a one-line description of each script. Do not run any script to determine the order. ## Stage 4: R packages and versions Run print_lockfile() from scripts/scan_packages.R. - If a lockfile exists, the Dependencies section states the R version, says that versions are pinned in renv.lock, gives the restore command renv::restore(), and includes the package table. - If no lockfile exists, the Dependencies section states that package versions were not recorded, and contains the placeholder from print_lockfile(). Do not guess versions or scan the installed library. ## Stage 5: Assemble, preview and reader-test Fill references/readme_template.md. Show the rendered Markdown in chat. Then read it as a newcomer who has only the repository and the paper: could they find the data, restore the environment, run the scripts in order and understand every variable? List any section still holding a placeholder. On confirmation, write README.md to the project root. ## Stage 6: Check the README against its sources If the project has tests/test_readme.R, run it in a fresh R session (Rscript -e "testthat::test_file('tests/test_readme.R')") and report the output verbatim. Otherwise compare the README yourself: the R and package versions against read_lockfile(), every numbered script against the scripts folder, and every unit against the user's answers. Report the number of placeholders left. ## AI declaration State that an AI assisted in generating this README, naming the model if the user wishes, with the date. Make no claims about AI use elsewhere in the project unless the user states them, and then record exactly what they state. ## Placeholders Write every unknown value as a visible placeholder, in exactly this form: **TODO: supply [field]: not provided** Flag a missing code licence and a missing code or data DOI as blocking for submission, but still write the file so the user has a working draft. ## Scope This skill does not audit code quality or reproducibility, and does not produce figures. If asked to do either mid-run, say so and stop that part of the request. ## References - Ivimey-Cook, E.R. et al. (2023) Implementing code review in the scientific workflow. Journal of Evolutionary Biology 36(10), 1347–1356. - Ivimey-Cook, E.R. et al. (2025) TADA! Simple guidelines to improve analytical code sharing for transparency and reproducibility. EcoEvoRxiv. ``` ::: ::: ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ### `references/readme_template.md` The Dependencies section is a single token, filled with one of the two versions defined in Stage 4 of `SKILL.md`, so the README is accurate whether or not a lockfile exists. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` markdown # {{TITLE}} {{DOI_BADGE}} {{LICENCE_BADGE}} ## Description {{DESCRIPTION}} ## Abstract {{ABSTRACT}} ## Instructions This repository contains the code and data accompanying the manuscript above. To reproduce the analysis: 1. Obtain the data as described under *Data files*. 2. Set up the R environment as described under *Dependencies*. 3. Run the scripts in the order given under *Scripts*. ## Authors | Name | ORCID | Affiliation | |------|-------|-------------| {{AUTHOR_ROWS}} ### Funding {{FUNDING}} ## Data files {{PER_FILE_SECTIONS}} ## Scripts Run in this order: | Order | Script | Description | |-------|--------|-------------| {{SCRIPT_ROWS}} ## Dependencies {{DEPENDENCIES}} ## Open questions {{OPEN_QUESTIONS}} ## AI declaration {{AI_DECLARATION}} ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Glossary ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
term definition
agent An assistant that can read across a project's files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises.
AI declaration A statement, for example in a README, recording that an AI assisted, naming the tool, model and date, and making no claim about AI use beyond what was recorded.
claimed execution A statement that code runs or reproduces, made without the command that was run and the output it produced. Treat it as a prediction, not evidence.
false positive In a code review, a problem the AI reports confidently that is not real, or describes wrongly.
rung One level of the autonomy ladder in Block 4, from suggesting a line (rung 0) to acting with no prompts (rung 5). Each step up removes a moment when you would have seen an action before it happened.
sentinel value A number with a special meaning, such as 9999 for "not recorded" or -1 for "run failed". It must be documented in a codebook and recoded before analysis.
````` ::: ::: ## References - **Ivimey-Cook, E.R., et al. (2023).** Implementing code review in the scientific workflow: insights from ecology and evolutionary biology. *Journal of Evolutionary Biology*, 36(10), 1347–1356. - **Ivimey-Cook, E.R., et al. (2025).** TADA! Simple guidelines to improve analytical code sharing for transparency and reproducibility. *EcoEvoRxiv* (preprint). - **Cihan, U., Haratian, V., İçöz, A., et al. (2025).** Automated code review in practice. *Proceedings of the 47th International Conference on Software Engineering: Software Engineering in Practice (ICSE-SEIP)*, 425–436. - **Cihan, U.
